reasoning: The extract gives extensive success measures, organised by strategic objective. Examples: "The Government will measure its success in establishing effective ACD by assessing progress towards the following outcomes" (phishing, malware blocking, rerouting), and similar lists for incidents, cyber crime, skills, growth and international work. It also says it will "define, analyse and present data which measures the state of our collective cyber security" and that the strategy will be "founded upon a rigorous and comprehensive set of metrics", with the NCSC playing a key role. On evaluation, it commits to "report back on progress made on an annual basis", to review the approach, and says Annex 3 outcomes "will be reviewed annually". That gives a timetable and some sense of reporting, which takes it past level 1. It also acknowledges the immaturity of cyber metrics and the lack of calibrated data, which partly explains why measurement is hard and why a metrics programme is needed. The strongest counter-example to level 2 is that many outcomes are vague ("significantly less vulnerable", "far larger proportion") with no baselines, targets or indicators. There is also no mention of piloting or testing the policy first, no independent evaluation design, and no consultation. Level 2 is reached because the measures are comprehensive and an annual reporting cycle is set out. Level 3 would need to explain why testing and evaluation methods were chosen, say whether the results will be published and what will happen to them, and name specific metrics with baselines and targets.
